quests.explanation: The suffix '-ment' turns a verb into a noun describing the result of the action — 'assign' becomes 'assignment.'
Compound words like this simply combine two complete words, keeping the double 's' from 'class.'

quests.hint: Remember all three syllables: LI-BRAR-Y, don't skip the middle 'r.'
quests.explanation: A common mispronunciation drops the second 'r,' but the correct spelling keeps both: L-I-B-R-A-R-Y.
The prefix 'sub-' means 'under,' and 'ject' comes from Latin 'jacere' (to throw) — together meaning something 'thrown under' for discussion.

quests.hint: Just three syllables: SE-MES-TER, single 's' throughout.
quests.explanation: This word comes from Latin 'sex' (six) and 'mensis' (month), referring to a roughly six-month academic term.
Like other compound words, this simply joins two familiar words without changing either spelling.
Compound words formed from two nouns, like 'textbook,' are almost always written as one word in modern English.

quests.hint: Tricky silent letters: SCHED-ULE, with the 'ch' often sounding like 'sk.'
quests.explanation: In American English, the 'ch' in 'schedule' is usually pronounced like 'sk,' which doesn't match the spelling — a word to memorize visually.
The suffix '-or' (instead of '-er') often appears after words ending in '-ate,' as in 'calculator' and 'narrator.'
When 'apply' becomes a noun, the 'y' changes to 'i' before adding '-cation' — a common pattern with verbs ending in '-y.'

quests.hint: Double 'e' at the end: EMPLOY + EE.
quests.explanation: The suffix '-ee' (meaning 'a person who receives the action') often doubles the final 'e,' as in 'employee' and 'trainee.'

quests.hint: Compare this to 'employee' — '-er' here means the person who gives the action.
quests.explanation: Notice the contrast: '-er' suffixes usually mean 'the one who does/gives,' while '-ee' suffixes mean 'the one who receives' the action.
The prefix 'inter-' means 'between,' so an interview is literally a 'view between' two people exchanging questions and answers.

quests.hint: This can mean both 'to continue' and 'a summary of your work history.'
quests.explanation: Context determines meaning here: 'resume' (continue) is a regular verb, while it's sometimes written 'résumé' with accents for the career-summary sense.
This word comes from Latin 'salarium,' originally referring to payment given to Roman soldiers for salt — a fun fact to help remember the spelling.
Borrowed from French, 'colleague' keeps an unusual 'eague' ending that doesn't follow typical English spelling patterns.
This vivid compound word originally referred to a literal line soldiers couldn't cross, now used for any final time limit.
The prefix 'over-' means 'beyond' or 'extra,' so 'overtime' is simply time worked beyond the normal schedule.
'Ware' means manufactured goods (as in 'hardware'), and 'software' contrasts with physical computer parts as the 'soft,' changeable programs.
This straightforward compound word describes a secret word that lets you 'pass' through to access something.
The suffix '-less' means 'without,' so 'wireless' simply means 'without wires' — useful for many other '-less' words like 'careless' and 'hopeless.'
This modern compound word uses the directional prefix 'down-' to describe transferring data from a larger system to your own device.
Compound technology words like this often combine an everyday object's name with the part it resembles or attaches to.
The prefix 'dis-' often means 'reverse' or 'reduce,' so a discount literally 'counts down' the original price.
This word has a silent 'p' before 't,' a leftover from its Latin origin 'recipere' — one to memorize by sight.
Someone who follows a regular 'custom' of buying from a particular shop became known as a 'customer' — a nice memory link for the spelling.
This word comes from the same root as 'guarantee,' and both share the double letter pattern that's easy to forget.
Adding '-y' to the verb 'deliver' creates the noun form, following the same simple pattern as 'discover' to 'discovery.'

quests.hint: Remember the 'ch' makes a 'sh' sound here: PUR-CHASE.
quests.explanation: Borrowed from French, 'purchase' keeps the French-style 'ch' pronounced as 'sh,' unlike the usual English 'ch' sound.

Despite looking related to 'invent' (create), 'inventory' actually comes from a different Latin root meaning 'a list of things found' — a good reminder that spelling patterns don't always match meaning.
